newsitem.title: USA: NASD to propose new govt securities pricing plan.
newsitem.headline: NASD to propose new govt securities pricing plan.

text.p: The National Association of Securities Dealers said Monday it will submit to Securities and Exchange Commission proposed rules for dealers to abide by when pricing the government securities they sell to investors.
The long-awaited rules, sought by Congress some four years ago, will provide dealers with guidance to help determine if the mark-ups they charge are fair.

Unlike the NASD standards established for stock sales, the rules won't give dealers specific percentages and benchmarks to use in government securities trades, John Ramsay, Deputy General Counsel of NASD Regulation Inc, told Reuters.

"The reason we haven't tried to specify a particular percentage is that an appropriate percentage will vary an awful lot depending upon what the particiular type of security is and the nature of the trading market," Ramsay said.
He said dealers would be required to consider several conditions before applying a mark-up, requiring them often to make such reviews case by case.
"We welcome the NASD's initiative," Paul Saltzman, Senior Vice President and General Counsel for PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, said.

"It's a huge issue for us. As we have said all along, PSA welcomes any guidance regulators can give in not only defining methodology by which one calculates prevailing market price, but guidance regarding the scope of a permissible mark-up," Saltzman said.

The proposed rule would help market participants determine the "prevailing market price" in different circumstances, NASD said. The prevailing market price is the baseline from which mark-up is calculated, NASD said.

Under the rule, the prevailing price would be based on the dealer's cost of acquiring the security, unless it can be shown that another measure is accurate, NASD proposed. Such an additional measure could include the price of a "similar" security, NASD said.
NASD's rule provides a list of factors that can be used to determine what is a similar security.
NASD said the steps dealers follow to calculate mark-ups in less frequently issued government securities, sucy as Fannie Maes, could vary.
